doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Not hiring women at first
summary: In grad school she never thought of hiring women and shared the stereotype; now Diva has few substitutes available.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: But I was in a position when I first started playing and recording and I mentioned about Michael Moore and I did get a chance to play with him on a CD. I would never hire a woman, ever. It didn’t even occur to me to hire a woman when I first started like doing my own projects and I was actually in grad school and I met my boyfriend John, we’re not together now, but he was a great alto player. We did two CDs together, did some recording. Never would it even have occurred to me for any reason to hire a woman. I mean nobody mentioned it. We’re just like let’s get these players we like and there wasn’t even a woman that would have come to my mind at all. Which is interesting. And even so I would have been skeptical just because, I don’t know if women will admit it, but I admit my ignorance too, thinking I had the stereotype too. And I was not like, I was different than the stereotype, so I’m serious and I want to be a really good player, and I’m not going to be one of those T&A women with the lipstick and short skirt trying to play jazz bad. You know play the sad version of “In the Mood” to make two hundred dollars in my miniskirt. So to me whenever I heard all-women bands I was like, you know, sure. So I became enlightened myself. And I also found though that like in the big band there’s fifteen players. We are extremely lucky if there’s one substitute for every chair. Just because the quality of the band is so high and there aren’t enough women to fill the chairs that play. And you go from the level of what the professional player is in Diva, and then like one notch down. I mean the gap is like this. It goes professional and very student. There’s not too much of a trickle up. It’s either you’re really, really good and you’ve taken it seriously or else you’re at a student level. With men it’s easy to call like twenty people right off the bat that are all equally qualified. So that’s a problem. © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-
